The clock on the tower at Orlen Cross stopped at ten past four one Tuesday in March. My grandfather, Aurel Moss, had kept it for forty-one years, climbing the worn iron ladder each Sunday to wind it, and that spring I had begun to climb with him. He had done the Sunday winding two days before, and on Monday the Harl bus had left by the clock to the minute.

We went up together after breakfast. A skin of ice still clung to the face, but the hands moved freely when he tried them, the weight cable sat snug on its drum, and every pin and part of the escapement was sound. Then he lifted his lamp to the gears. Two pigeons had built a nest of twigs and bus tickets between the teeth of the great wheel, and two eggs sat in it, looking thoroughly at home.

At the council meeting that evening, Jonas Brede from the hardware shop brought a catalogue of new electric works to replace the old, and had already bolted a scaffold to the tower. He spoke of their low cost and of my grandfather's safety on the ladder. Petra Vell, who chaired the council and keeps a bird feeder in every window, had borrowed my grandfather's notebook. She read out an entry from 1991: pigeons in the great wheel, April, left until fledged. Then she read it again and called the vote.

The council voted six to one to leave the nest and its birds where they were. Jonas struck his scaffold the next morning, pole by pole, and stacked the poles in his van, while a small crowd on the bakery steps offered him advice.

For most of April the clock said ten past four. The Harl bus ran by the driver's watch, the spring fair opened to a cheer where the bell should have been, and people took to asking one another the time, which led to a great deal of conversation. In May the chicks flew, and my grandfather swept out the twigs and wound the clock. He handed the bus tickets to the driver, who swore one was his.

passage:
Lune's starwort, a pale blue flower about the size of a thumbnail, grows only on the north slope of Corrow Ridge. For a decade its seed heads have come up nearly empty, a serious matter for a plant that lives only four or five years. In 2023 the park's warden, Petra Moss, asked Ines Varga, an ecologist at Pellham University, to find out why.

Everyone at Corrow had an explanation. Moss blamed the sheep; her proof was the 1988 photograph in her office, taken the summer before Aldo Brisk first drove his flock up: the slope blue to the crest. On the strength of it, the board has kept the flock off the slope until August since 2016. Brisk, who has grazed the slope for more than thirty years, blamed the late frosts. Varga decided to test every idea at once. Her student, Tobin Hale, staked out twenty-five plots where the starwort still grew thickest. Some were fenced against the sheep, some sheltered under cloths on frosty nights, some watered in dry weeks to keep the soil moist through the summer, and some cleared of crowding grass. On the last set Hale did the bees' work himself with a paintbrush, dabbing pollen from flower to flower.

In September Ruth Callan, who teaches at the village school in Ottery, brought her pupils up to count seeds. One set of plots stood out: the cleared plots held about forty seeds a head, against four or five everywhere else on the slope. The grass, it turned out, had grown tall enough to smother the starwort, because since 2016 nothing had grazed it in spring.

The board met in October and, having spent eight years keeping the sheep away to save the starwort, voted, amid some laughter, to bring them back to save the starwort. From next year Brisk will take his flock up in May.

Moss has kept the photograph on her wall, where it still shows what the board is hoping for: starwort enough to cover the slope again. Brisk has asked whether, in fairness, it might now hang in his kitchen instead. The minutes record the affair in a single solemn line.
